analysis.one_liner: Requires the consumer financial watchdog to get each person's advance permission before examining their financial records.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee on a 32-25 vote in November 2013 and was reported to the House in February 2014, but never received a vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend Dodd-Frank so the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau could not request, access, collect, use, retain, or disclose a consumer's nonpublic personal information unless the Bureau first told the consumer exactly what it wanted and the consumer affirmatively allowed it. The same rules would apply to any contractor collecting data for the CFPB, and the bill would strip the CFPB's exemption from the Right to Financial Privacy Act of 1978, subjecting its examinations to that law's procedures. Supporters framed it as protecting consumers' financial privacy; critics said it would hobble the CFPB's ability to police banks and lenders for fraud and abuse.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries would be banks, lenders, debt collectors, and other companies supervised by the CFPB, which would face a regulator far less able to pull their customers' records during examinations and investigations. Consumers gain a notification-and-consent right over the watchdog's use of their personal data, but because the consent must come affirmatively before any collection, the practical effect is to blunt data-driven supervision that uncovers fraud and abuse affecting consumers. Privacy-minded consumers who distrust government data collection get a genuine procedural protection.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks and lenders under CFPB oversight

how_it_helps.text: Consumers would receive a clear written or electronic disclosure of what nonpublic personal information the CFPB intends to request, and could withhold permission before any collection occurs.

The Right to Financial Privacy Act's procedural protections — notice and an opportunity to challenge disclosures of financial records — would again cover CFPB examinations, since the bill repeals the CFPB's exemption from that 1978 law.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers would pay indirectly: the CFPB's core tool is examining firms' records to find patterns of fraud, discriminatory lending, and abusive debt collection, and requiring advance consumer consent for nonpublic personal information would make that supervision much harder. Privacy would be protected in name while the agency charged with catching industry-wide abuses lost much of its reach.

drawbacks.text: Requiring advance notice and affirmative permission from each consumer before the CFPB could collect nonpublic personal information would have made routine, data-driven supervision of lenders and debt collectors impractical, hampering detection of fraud and abusive practices that individual consumers cannot see on their own.

The bill was drafted to weaken an active regulator: it expanded the bar from 'obtain' to requesting, accessing, collecting, using, retaining, or disclosing information, and applied the restriction to CFPB contractors, going beyond a simple privacy notice.

The CFPB already was barred from obtaining personally identifiable financial information without meeting statutory conditions; the bill added restrictions on top of an existing prohibition rather than closing a gap in consumer protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protections sound appealing, but the consumer-permission requirement would have seriously impaired the CFPB's ability to detect patterns of abuse across millions of accounts — the kind of harm consumers cannot see on their own. A single informed opt-out for examiners, as the Bureau requested, could have addressed the main concern without handcuffing supervision; this bill went further than that. The benefit to everyday consumers is speculative; the cost in weakened enforcement is concrete.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill and put it on the Union Calendar, but House leadership never brought it to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced June 28, 2013 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee.

The Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit held a hearing on October 29, 2013, and the full committee marked up the bill on November 21, 2013, ordering it reported by a 32-25 vote.
The committee reported the bill without amendment on February 6, 2014 (H. Rept. 113-344), and it was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 254.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a House floor vote and died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and consumer finance companies that opposed CFPB data access benefit, since the constraint on the regulator never became law but also never faced a recorded floor vote. Consumer privacy interests gained nothing tangible.

sides.party_line_note: All seven cosponsors were Republicans, and the committee's 32-25 vote to report the bill split largely along party lines, with every recorded supporter a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would sharply restrict the CFPB's ability to request, access, collect, or use consumers' nonpublic personal information during examinations and enforcement, requiring advance disclosure and affirmative consumer permission first. It would also subject the Bureau to the Right to Financial Privacy Act, stripping its Dodd-Frank examination exemption.

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, and consumer financial companies under CFPB supervision
industries.note: Regulated financial firms gain because the watchdog would face notice-and-consent hurdles before examining consumers' nonpublic personal information held by these companies. Firms under investigation for consumer harm benefit from a weakened examiner.
